tracks.title: Which command makes it a URL?
tracks.text: Lesson one point eight — publishing. A sub-lesson, under workbook. The parent lesson ended with a complete, self-contained file — shop dot html. You can double-click it. The document is the deployment. So now there's one obvious next move… get it a public link. And here every reflex you trained on twenty years of web development fires at once. A platform account. A CI pipeline. A build step on the host. Environment variables. The whole apparatus of deployment. [curious] Then the vocabulary trips you. Workbooks has a deploy command too. So which one do you run to get a URL — publish… or deploy? This page kills that confusion in the first screen. Because the reason publishing needs none of that apparatus… is that the apparatus was for turning source into a running app on someone else's machine. And you don't have source to build. You have a finished file. The build already happened… in your hand… before any of this.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. To publish is to put an already-assembled workbook on a surface — a website or host. Distribution only. And it's distinct from deploy, which converges the runtime engine. The split is by object. Publish acts on the workbook. Deploy acts on the engine. [curious] And the CLI's taxonomy enforces that on purpose, because the two verbs once collided. The old publish command both rendered org into HTML… and shipped it. That got resolved — so that bundle renders and assembles, and publish only ships. Picture the lifecycle as a spine, left to right. First, author. Second, build. Third, bundle. Fourth, run. Fifth, publish — ending at a URL, the file on a surface. And then deploy hangs off to the side, on a dotted line, pointed not at the workbook but at the engine. It's about the machine… not the document. You reach for it only when running the thing needs a live runtime at all. And most published workbooks… never do.

tracks.title: The declared surface
tracks.text: Next — publish dot org, the declared surface. Publishing is declared, not configured by flags. You write one file that names where the workbook should land… and the CLI converges on that declaration. It's the same declare-then-converge motion the deploy kit uses, so both halves of the system feel like one idea. Here's the scaffold the CLI writes, read aloud. Title… Workbooks publish config. Publish target… cloudflare-pages. Publish project… my-workbook. And a few comment lines that document the choices — target is cloudflare-pages, gh-pages, or self-hosted; project is the CF Pages project name, a GitHub repo, or a runtime URL; domain is an optional custom domain for the printed URL. And the last comment says it plainly — publish apply ships the assembled workbook, run bundle first, publish is distribution only. Now the part that matters about that file. It is inert. It's read by a lenient keyword scanner… not by the kernel that runs your workbook's logic. It just collects the keyword lines into one table. Your publish file cannot execute anything. It's a label describing a destination… nothing more. Three properties carry the whole thing. First, publish target — which door, one of three. Second, publish project — the address at that door. Third, publish domain — and here's the trick: it's print-time only. It changes the URL the CLI reports… never where the bytes actually go. Hold on to that last fact. It answers a question people ask later.

tracks.title: Init, validate, apply
tracks.text: Init… validate… apply. Three verbs, one motion — declare, check, converge. First, init writes the scaffold. Run it once. If a publish file already exists, it refuses rather than clobber your config, and on success it tells you the next move — wrote publish dot org, edit it, then publish apply. Second, validate is a coherence check with no side effects. It confirms the target is one of the three known doors and the project isn't empty. Nothing shipped. If the door is unknown it says the target must be cloudflare-pages, gh-pages, or self-hosted. If the address is blank it says publish project is required. Clean, it prints what it read back — ok, publish dot org, target cloudflare-pages, project shop. Third, apply is the convergence — the only verb that touches a surface. It takes the workbook to ship, defaulting to workbook dot html, and ends with a single line… published, then the workbook, then an arrow, then the URL. Under apply the mechanics are humble. The artifact is written as index dot html into a throwaway temp directory, that directory is handed to the right door, the URL is printed, and the temp dir is removed. One workbook becomes one index dot html… becomes one URL. Picture the whole flow as a graph. Init lays down the file. You edit it. Validate is the fork where two failures can send you back — an unknown target, or an empty project — and the clean path leads to apply. Apply has its own early exit if no config exists. Otherwise the staged file goes to whichever door you named… and the URL is printed. Every failure edge… is the real error string.

tracks.title: Why org is refused
tracks.text: Why is org refused? Here's the error a reader will actually hit — and it's worth hitting on purpose, because it's where the whole lesson lands. Hand publish a raw org file and it refuses, flatly — error… publish ships assembled workbooks, run bundle first. [curious] This is the resolved collision, made visible. Publish does not render. That job belongs to bundle, which lints and assembles your org source into a runnable file. Publish ships what's already finished. So the fix is one step earlier in the spine — run bundle, then publish the result. And notice publish happily takes a wbundle. It opens it as the plain zip it is, pulls workbook dot html out by name, and ships that. A bare html file ships as-is. So the input rule has three cases. First, hand it a workbook dot html — it ships as-is, already assembled. Second, hand it a wbundle — it gets unzipped in memory, and the inner workbook dot html ships. Third, hand it an org file — refused, run bundle first. The verdict across those three… is the whole thesis. Assembly happens before the doorstep… never on it. The html and the wbundle are finished. The org isn't, so it's turned away. Publish is distribution. Bundle is assembly. And the guard exists so the two can never quietly merge back into one verb again.

tracks.title: Three doors, one motion
tracks.text: Three doors, one motion. This is the centerpiece. Three targets, the same declare-then-converge motion behind all of them — and they're dumb on purpose. Because the file is smart. A static host, a git branch, and a raw HTTP PUT can all accept the same workbook… because the workbook needs nothing from them but a place to sit. Picture the apply fanning out. The CLI always does the same first move — stage the workbook as index dot html. Then, depending on the target, one of three doors opens. First door — cloudflare-pages. The CLI shells out to wrangler, deploying the staged directory under your project name, and prints a pages dot dev URL. Second door — gh-pages. And here the mechanics are blunt, worth knowing before you lean on them. The CLI makes a fresh git repo on a gh-pages branch, commits as a bot user with the message wbx publish, and then force-pushes that single-commit branch. The URL is your github dot io page. Read the force-push honestly — that branch is an artifact surface, not a place to keep history. Each publish overwrites it. Third door — self-hosted. The CLI issues a single PUT to slash w slash your slug, carrying the artifact bytes, with an optional bearer token from the environment. The printed URL is that same path. And this is the door that's not dumb — it's an engine. It gets its own section next.

tracks.title: Publishing into your engine
tracks.text: Publishing into your engine. The first two doors are storage — a static host, a git branch. They hold bytes and hand them back. The self-hosted door is different in kind. The surface is a Nexus… a live engine. And this is the one case where the words publish and the engine touch… without becoming the same verb. Publish still only ships a finished artifact — it just ships it to something that can do more than serve it flat. Picture the round trip. First, with your token in the environment, the CLI PUTs the artifact to slash w slash shop. Second, the engine stores it and answers two-oh-one, stored. Third, the CLI prints the URL. Then later, a visitor does a GET on the same path… and the engine serves the workbook back. And because it's a live engine answering each request, it can gate that request… hold the auth… run live state. The bearer you present is simply the token your engine accepts. If you stood that engine up yourself, it's the bearer your deploy minted for it. [curious] And that's the whole reason this lane exists. A static-hosted workbook is exactly as alive as the file — which is to say, not. If you want per-request gating, schedules, agents, or multiplayer… you don't publish onto a dumb surface. You publish into an engine. Same three verbs… same finished artifact… a smarter doorstep.

tracks.title: What may never go on a static host
tracks.text: Now the honest part — what may never go on a static host. This is the question that actually keeps people up. Is my data safe on a public host? [sighs] The honest answer is a flat no — unless the workbook's posture is public. A static host ships the whole file to anyone who asks. Any gating drawn on top of inlined data is decoration… not security. Every workbook route carries one of three postures, and only one is safe to bake into a public static file. First, public — allowed everywhere, because there's nothing to leak. Second, gated data — refused by the static doors, because they'd ship the data to everyone; allowed only self-hosted, where the engine gates per request. Third, gated route — same story, refused on a static host, allowed only through the engine. The verdict of that grid… a gated workbook may only go through the self-hosted door, where a live engine can refuse each request. And the runtime's own validator says it in words — client-side gating is theater. There's a smaller hygiene guard too. Validate warns if a property key looks like a secret — anything ending in token, key, secret, account, password, or credential — or if a value looks like a long hex ID. It tells you to use an environment variable instead of storing it in the file. That's why the self-hosted bearer comes from the environment… and never from the config. One honest seam — today this enforcement lives on the runtime side. The Rust lane validates only the target and project. So the guarantee is real… but it's the engine that holds it. Treat a gated workbook as self-hosted-only… whichever lane you reach for.

tracks.title: Where publish ends
tracks.text: Where publish ends. Honesty section — five edges worth knowing before you lean on them. First — gh-pages is a force-push. Each publish writes a fresh single-commit branch and force-pushes it, destroying whatever history was there. Fine for an artifact surface… but don't keep anything on that branch you'd miss. Second — one file, one URL. Publish maps one workbook to one index dot html to one URL. Multi-page sites are a different mode entirely, a runtime-side manifest that renders a list of pages into a flat directory. A separate tool… not a flag. Third — a published static workbook is inert. It's exactly as alive as the file. No schedules, no agents, no live state. That's what docking into an engine is for. Fourth — publish domain doesn't configure DNS. It changes only the URL the CLI prints. The actual custom-domain wiring happens at the host — the Cloudflare dashboard, a GitHub Pages CNAME. Setting it makes the printed link match where your DNS already points… it does not point your DNS. And fifth — two publish surfaces exist, and ships-only is the canon. The Rust lane ships only. An older Elixir lane still renders org into HTML before shipping, and adds a fourth target that scaffolds a desktop app. That render step predates the collision fix. When these pages say publish ships and bundle renders… they mean the canon.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Do viewers need anything installed? No. A published workbook is a static HTML file. Anyone with a browser opens the URL and it runs — the runtime is bound inside the file. Can I publish straight from workbook dot org? No — bundle first. Hand publish an org file and it refuses, run bundle first. How do I update a published workbook? Re-run apply. It's idempotent convergence to the same declaration — same target, same project, same URL. You don't tear down and recreate… you re-converge. Where do I set up my custom domain? At the host. The domain property only changes the URL the CLI prints — it does no DNS wiring. Can I password-protect a published workbook? Not on a static host — and that's not a missing feature, it's the truth about static hosting. The file is the whole workbook. To actually gate, the posture must be gated and it must go through the self-hosted door. And — publish versus deploy, one more time? Publish puts a finished workbook on a surface. Deploy converges an engine on infrastructure. Different objects… different axes. You publish a document. You deploy a machine.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that's publishing. Not deployment in disguise — distribution only. Because the artifact is already finished software, putting it online reduces to one thing… one file becomes index dot html somewhere, and that's a URL. The targets are dumb on purpose, because the file is smart. [curious] The way back up is short. This sub-lesson sits under workbook — lesson one — the artifact this verb ships. And right beside it is bundles, the assembly step publish refuses to do for you. Read those two… and the doorstep makes complete sense.
